title: Colour, Light, and Materiality: Biophilic Interior Design Presence in Research and Practice
review_question: What evidence for colour, light, and materiality can support biophilic design?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Empirical research articles related to biophilic attributes, colour, light, and materiality, published in English between 1978 and 2018. Articles were scored based on relevance to both interior design and biophilic features (70% agreement threshold for inclusion).

search_databases: Referex Engineering—Materials and Mechanical Collection (Engineering Village)

synthesis_conclusions: The literature review identified 18 biophilic attributes related to colour, light, and materiality, with engagement and preference being the most frequently identified themes.
The top attributes shared by both the literature review and practitioners were abstraction of nature, composition, natural light, and natural materials.
There is a focus on biophilic attributes in both research and practice, but many attributes are not yet linked to research or widely used in practice.
Colour, light, and materiality are complex and interrelated concepts that are thoughtfully used by interior designers to fulfill project goals and biophilic design.
evidence_gaps: Many biophilic attributes have not been linked to research or are not being used in practice.
Further inquiry is needed to better understand how biophilic design can be more diversely integrated for optimal nature-like interior environments.
Direct linkages between colour and health outcomes are still under-researched, with insufficient evidence for causal relationships between specific paint colours and patient healthcare outcomes.
Additional research is needed on the ability of designers to use natural materials and connect to the local environment through material selection.
More research is warranted on the psychological benefits of indoor plants due to heterogeneity in existing results.
Concerns for infection, litigation, and maintenance may be holding back increased indoor plant use.
A larger, targeted systematic review of each feature (colour, light, materiality) is needed to draw additional research together for designers.
risk_of_bias_assessment: internal scoring system based on relevance criteria (70% agreement threshold for inclusion of articles related to both biophilic design and interior design)
limitations: The review was limited and targeted, serving as an important starting point rather than a comprehensive overview.

paper_metadata.title: Colour, Light, and Materiality: Biophilic Interior Design Presence in Research and Practice
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Colour, Light, and Materiality: Biophilic Interior Design Presence in Research and Practice
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The biophilic design hypothesis uses nature-based environmental design for optimising people’s health and well-being. Stephen Kellert in 2008 developed a list of biophilic attributes that was further refined in the Biophilic Interior Design Matrix (BID-M) to specifically support the interior application of biophilic design for health and well-being. The present study further investigates biophilic interior design using the BID-M language and the key interior design components colour, light, and materiality. The first part of the study reviewed four decades of literature related to biophilia and colour, light, and materiality to investigate a total of 19 publications. The second part of the study explored the perceptions of 23 design practitioners' and the use of biophilia related to colour, light, and materiality in their practice. For the first time, evidence was identified about colour, light, and materiality being linked to biophilic design and the attributes in the BID-M. The study results showed colour preferences were the most frequently identified theme, and practitioners used a variety of biophilic attributes in their practice. The top attributes shared by both the literature review and practitioners were the abstraction of nature, composition, natural light, and natural materials. This finding shows that there is a focus on biophilic attributes in both research and practice, however, there are still many attributes that have not been linked to research and are not being used in practice. Further inquiry is needed to better understand how biophilic design can be more diversely integrated for optimal nature-like interior environments.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments restore directed attention better than urban environments, leading to reduced mental fatigue and improved cognitive function.
Exposure to natural environments reduces physiological and psychological stress, promoting recovery and well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper synthesizes how specific biophilic elements, particularly natural light and visual connections to nature, contribute to human well-being by engaging cognitive restorative processes and regulating physiological functions.

steps.from_construct: Visual connection to nature (e.g., views of greenery, natural patterns)
steps.to_construct: Reduced mental fatigue and improved cognitive function

steps.from_construct: Access to natural light (e.g., daylighting, dynamic light)
steps.to_construct: Improved mood and regulated sleep-wake cycles
